It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing (klaxon.faults).

case.name: pool-exhaustion
case.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500.
case.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

fault.name: pool-exhaustion
fault.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry

expected_symptoms: the pool runs dry about 40 to 50 s after the deploy; then POST /payments takes 5 to 8 s (a worker thread, then the pool's 5 s wait) and fails with a 500: the p95 latency passes 7 s, and the 5xx share passes 70% within a minute
the payments API logs 'unhandled error' with PoolTimeout: no connection within 5 s
its health check fails too, so docker marks it unhealthy, while PostgreSQL itself is up
the traffic's clients retry and give up: many payments end with their outcome unknown, and arrivals past 64 in flight are shed
the money check passes: a payment that never got a connection was never charged, and one charged before its answer was lost is confirmed by its webhook
fault.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

diagnosis.hypothesis: payments-api's PostgreSQL connection pool (psycopg_pool) is exhausted, so requests wait about 5 s for a connection and then fail with PoolTimeout (HTTP 500). That explains both the 5xx rate and the p95 latency of about 7 s. The pool drained right after payments-api was redeployed at 06:55:25 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. Refunds are the likely culprit: they run 5 to 7.7 s and also end in PoolTimeout. Provider calls stay fast (p95 about 5 ms), so connections are not being held across slow provider calls. More likely, the refund path keeps its connections and never returns them to the pool, so the pool empties and every route times out. Two things remain open. The deploy log shows only the new settings, so I cannot confirm that REFUND_CONNECTION was different before. I also saw no pool or PostgreSQL connection count, which is what would prove the leak.

evidence.shows: payments-api 500s appear suddenly in the latest point (3.44/s) while 201s fall, which confirms the alert's symptom.
payments-api was redeployed at 06:55:25, about 1 minute before the 500s, with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. Every other service was created at 06:53:59 and has not changed since.
The errors on POST /payments are all psycopg_pool PoolTimeout: the database connection pool is exhausted.
A failed POST /payments spends about 5 s between its Redis idempotency SET and EVAL with no DB span, then returns 500 PoolTimeout. That gap is waiting for a pool connection.
Many POST /payments/{id}/refunds requests take 5 to 7.7 s, starting from about 06:55:53, shortly after the deploy.
A refund also fails with PoolTimeout after 7.7 s, so the pool starvation affects refunds as well.
payments-api's calls to the provider stay fast (p95 about 5 ms), so the provider is not the cause and connections are not being held across slow provider calls.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to its settings from before the 06:55:25 deploy, most likely restoring the previous REFUND_CONNECTION behaviour. Recreating the container also releases any leaked connections. Afterwards, watch the 5xx rate and latency of POST /payments and refunds. Run the money check to confirm that refunds which failed with 500s did not leave our records and the provider's out of step.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api pauses while its container is recreated, so in-flight payment and refund requests fail and clients must retry. Idempotency keys in Redis should prevent double charges on those retries. If the previous settings had their own defect, it returns. Refunds that already reached the provider but errored on our side are not repaired by the rollback.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: Redeploy payments-api with the current settings (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents). If the pool still exhausts after the rollback, look elsewhere: check PostgreSQL connection counts and max_connections, and look for long-running transactions.
